Trump is weighing new strikes on Iran as Israel presses for a joint air campaign. Separately, a tanker was hit in the Strait of Hormuz and a Houthi missile threat caused damage in Riyadh. Brent briefly topped $93 before settling around $92. Gold futures slipped about 0.4%, in line with the war-time pattern of escalation feeding Fed hike bets. AUD/USD fell about 0.6% to near 0.6680 after Australian unemployment jumped to 4.9% and jobs fell 43,500, missing on every measure. The USD was firmer more broadly. BOJ Governor Ueda said the bank expects to keep raising rates, with real rates still low and inflation at risk of overshooting. JGB yields still eased. AI stocks stayed under scrutiny after Moody’s cut Nvidia’s outlook. Goldman cut its KOSPI target to 7,500 but stays bullish, and Sony rose on the “GTA VI” launch. Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 and debuts on the Nasdaq as ANT later Thursday. Bitcoin fell about 1% to around $63,700. Oil traders spent Asia’s session weighing fresh signs of escalation across the Gulf. The New York Times reported that President Trump is considering another round of extensive strikes on Iran, with Israel pressing Washington to join a four- to seven-day air campaign, although no decision has been made and the administration is divided. A loaded tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile while sailing outbound through the Strait of Hormuz, and Reuters reported that a Saudi-led coalition dealt with a Houthi missile aimed at Riyadh, with debris causing material damage, shortly after Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met the head of US Central Command. With the Houthis also pushing toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, both of the region’s key shipping chokepoints are under threat. Brent briefly traded above $93 before paring gains to hold around $92, while WTI hovered near $82. Gold slipped, with futures down about 0.4% near $3,730 after a brief dip below $3,700. That fits the pattern seen throughout this war: escalation lifts oil, higher oil feeds inflation fears, and that strengthens the case for further Fed hikes, which weighs on gold rather than sending it higher as a haven. Australia: jobs shock sinks the Aussie The Australian dollar was the session’s biggest mover after a jobs report that missed on every line. Unemployment jumped to 4.9% from 4.7%, the highest since late 2021, as employment fell 43,500 against forecasts of a 25,000 gain, a second straight monthly decline. Part-time and full-time jobs both fell, and unemployment rose even as participation dropped to 66.6%. The data back the three RBA board members who opposed November’s hike to 4.85% and look likely to take further rate increases off the table. AUD/USD fell from around 0.6720 to as low as 0.6662 and was trading near 0.6680, down about 0.6%. The US dollar was firmer more broadly, though moves elsewhere were modest. EUR/USD edged lower toward 1.0965 and USD/JPY rose to around 159.6, keeping the yen close to the 160 level despite another hawkish turn from the Bank of Japan. Japan: Ueda keeps the hiking path open BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda said the bank expects to keep raising rates because monetary conditions remain accommodative, warning that underlying inflation risks overshooting the 2% target. He added that real rates are still low at the short end, that strong earnings and rising wages should help firms absorb higher costs, and that the drop in third-quarter consumption was within the bank’s expectations. A Reuters poll showed 86% of economists expect a hike to 1.50% at the December 17 to 18 meeting. Japanese government bond yields nonetheless eased, with the 10-year down about 4 basis points to around 2.83%. September core machinery orders rose 13.4% from a year earlier, close to forecasts, pointing to firm business investment demand. Fed backdrop Overnight, four Federal Reserve officials, Christopher Waller, Neel Kashkari, Mary Daly and Michael Barr, all leaned toward further tightening, with Waller arguing for a 50 basis point hike in December to break the perception that 3% inflation is the norm. Markets are pricing roughly 61 basis points of hikes over the next three meetings, but give a half point move in December little chance. The US 10-year yield held near 5.05%. Separately, Moody’s kept the US at Aa1 with a stable outlook, noting the economy has outperformed its expectations. AI and tech: reassessment continues The AI trade remained under scrutiny after Nvidia’s turmoil. Moody’s cut its outlook on Nvidia to stable from positive following Jensen Huang’s resignation, while the company’s leadership told staff at an all-hands meeting that its strategy and roadmap remain intact, though the board chair conceded there is no Huang clone. Japanese AI-linked stocks are losing their valuation premium, with Kioxia and Advantest down more than 9% since Huang’s exit. Goldman Sachs cut its KOSPI target to 7,500 from 9,000 but still sees about 48% upside and stays overweight Korea. Sony was a bright spot, rising almost 3% in Tokyo on the global launch of “Grand Theft Auto VI”, with about three-quarters of an estimated 17 million copies sold on PlayStation. Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 per share, above its $70 to $78 range, selling 980 million shares in a deal worth around $81 billion. The stock is due to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT later on Thursday, with no scheduled time for the first trade. Elon Musk said Anthropic wants as much as 10 gigawatts of extra compute from SpaceX, a claim the company has not confirmed. Equities Regional markets were mixed. The Nikkei 225 rose about 0.5% to around 59,300 while the broader TOPIX closed flat. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell about 2% and the Shanghai Composite slipped 0.4%. The KOSPI swung through the session, dropping around 2% at its low before recovering to trade little changed, with SK Hynix up about 1.5%. US equity index futures were firmer, with Nasdaq 100 futures up about 1% and S&P 500 futures up around 0.6%. Crypto Bitcoin fell about 1% to around $63,700. BlackRock has been pitching bitcoin as an asset that moves independently of stocks, but November’s decoupling has mostly meant bitcoin missing the equity rebound rather than providing a hedge. Lava chief executive Shehzan Maredia said selling by miners and large holders has largely run its course, setting up a potential recovery, but on-chain data show large holders sending about $55 million more bitcoin to exchanges each day than they withdraw. Ahead US weekly jobless claims and the Philadelphia Fed survey are due at 13:30 GMT (8:30 am US Eastern), with Walmart results before the US open. Anthropic’s debut follows, and Japan’s October national CPI is due at 23:30 GMT (6:30 pm US Eastern). This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.content: AI is moving from experiments to everyday work. Users are working across browsers, virtual desktops, SaaS platforms, and cloud services, while agents are starting to act on their behalf. IT teams must keep pace by strengthening resilience, controlling costs, supporting distributed environments, and extending security into operational technology. That puts a familiar piece of infrastructure under new scrutiny: the endpoint. IGEL Now & Next 2027 will bring together CIOs, CISOs, EUC leaders, architects, partners, and technology innovators to explore how enterprise IT leaders are solving the ever-changing challenges in their endpoint security architecture. Here are eight reasons why you need to be there. 1. AI changes the risk equation Enterprise AI is opening doors and creating new paths to enterprise data and services through apps, browsers, copilots, and agents. For IT leaders, the question is no longer “How do we adopt AI?” It’s “How do we stay in control as we do?” At Now & Next 2027, expect a closer look at the governed endpoint foundation enterprises need to support AI as applications and access models evolve. 2. Stronger security starts at the endpoint Security teams have spent years hardening identities, networks, cloud services, applications, and detection. The endpoint can’t remain the weak link. At Now & Next, industry experts will explore prevention-first approaches that reduce endpoint attack surface while strengthening the role of the device in Zero Trust-aligned architectures. Zero Trust depends on enforcing policy where work happens. Attendees will see how IGEL works with identity, SSE/SASE, enterprise browsers, VDI, DaaS, and security tools to turn policy into access decisions. 3. When systems go down, work goes on Most organizations have invested heavily in recovering infrastructure, applications, and data. But when a cyberattack, failed update, or operating system incident affects thousands of employee devices, another question appears: How quickly can users get back to work? That endpoint recovery gap is becoming a board-level resilience issue. Now & Next 2027 will put business continuity at the center of the endpoint conversation: keeping critical applications accessible while response and recovery teams restore affected environments. 4. EUC strategy catches up with the modern enterprise Modern work is no longer defined by a single desktop architecture. Microsoft Azure Virtual Desktop, Windows 365, Citrix, Omnissa, SaaS, enterprise browsers, local applications, and cloud services increasingly coexist inside the same enterprise. The result can be extraordinary flexibility. It can also create operational complexity. Now & Next brings that ecosystem into one conversation. 5. Industry conversations go vertical Endpoint architectures look very different inside a hospital, a bank, a public-sector agency, a contact center, or a manufacturing facility. Healthcare leaders must protect sensitive data without interrupting care. Financial institutions face rigorous governance and audits. Public-sector organizations confront sophisticated threats. Manufacturers must secure access without slowing production. Expect industry-focused discussions built around the actual environments CIOs, CISOs, and infrastructure leaders are responsible for. 6. OT enters the spotlight Operational technology brings a different set of priorities to endpoint strategy. On the plant floor, in control rooms, and across critical infrastructure, uptime, resilience, and secure access matter differently because disruption can stop operations. As IT and OT converge, the OT track at Now & Next will explore how organizations can strengthen endpoint trust, governance, segmentation, and operational resilience without adding unnecessary complexity. The question is simple: How do you modernize access without destabilizing the operations you depend on? 7. A new home in Fort Lauderdale Now & Next 2027 lands at the newly opened Omni Fort Lauderdale, a waterfront setting built with modern meeting spaces, rooftop views, restaurants, and plenty of places to keep the conversation going. And when the sessions wrap, Fort Lauderdale’s beaches, waterways, dining, and nightlife are close by. 8. And yes to the afterparty! Every Now & Next ends with a bang. In Fort Lauderdale, it’ll be one for the books! You’ve worked hard, and this is where the community celebrates what’s next. Make sure you’re a part of it. Join the CIOs, CISOs, EUC leaders, architects, partners, and practitioners shaping that answer at IGEL Now & Next 2027. Register today.

articles.title: Campaigners save historic WW2 huts in Ripon which helped ‘save lives and win the war’
articles.desc: “What better buildings in which to inspire young people with an interest in science than those in which helped save lives and win us the Second World War”
articles.content: Delight as Ripon’s historic WW2 huts are finally saved from demolition Campaigners save historic WW2 huts in Ripon which helped ‘save lives and win the war’ “What better buildings in which to inspire young people with an interest in science than those in which helped save lives and win us the Second World War” Campaigners say they are delighted that their long battle to save historic Second World War huts at a former military camp in Ripon credited with “saving lives and winning the war” has at last paid off. For the past three years Ripon Military Heritage Trust has been campaigning to save some of the huts at Deverell Barracks in Ripon. During the Second World War, the huts housed Ripon’s School of Military Engineering which played critical role in the Allied victory over the Nazis. Demolition of the last surviving intact, 1939 wooden-hutted Militia Camp in the country had been due to begin early in the New Year. But a delighted Ripon Military Heritage Trust says that Homes England, which now owns the site, has agreed to dismantle rather than demolish two of these huts and give them to the Trust instead. Guy Wilson, Chairman of RMHT, said: “We are most grateful to Homes England for giving us this opportunity to preserve these unique buildings. “Now the work begins to store them safely and work with planners, politicians and the community to find an appropriate site on which to rebuild them to tell Ripon’s fascinating military history. “What better buildings in which to inspire young people with an interest in science and technology than those in which, during the Second World War, allied engineers learnt the skills that saved lives and win us the war.” The huts chosen to be saved, the Lecture hut and one of the two Instruction huts, are the only known examples of their type. They are the huts in which British and allied army engineers were trained during the Second World War. Homes England is giving RMHT the opportunity to dismantle and retain the four Cold War metal “Twynham huts” on the barracks site before demolition begins in the New Year. RMHT has also been allowed to select and retain moveable items ranging from beds and cupboards to a cell door and an air raid siren to facilitate future interpretation of the barracks. Tom Baker, Senior Planning & Enabling Manager at Homes England, said: “We recognise Ripon Military Heritage Trust's ambition to create an educational facility that reflects the history of the site and are pleased to have been able to contribute to that effort. “As part of our planning for the redevelopment of Deverell Barracks, we have worked with the RMHT to make a range of original materials available for reuse, including former military buildings, furniture and documents.” Ripon Military Heritage Trust (RMHT) is a charitable incorporated organisation (registered charity no. 1203294) founded in 2023 to research, conserve, interpret and provide access to the military heritage of Ripon and its surroundings. It is run by unpaid volunteer trustees. Its chairman, Guy Wilson, is a former Master of the Royal Armouries. Iconic Media Group Ltd. All rights reserved.

articles.title: EU aims for 20% boost in advanced materials leadership by 2035
articles.content: EU aims for 20% boost in advanced materials leadership by 2035 EU aims for 20% boost in advanced materials leadership by 2035 EU aims for 20% boost in advanced materials leadership by 2035 The European Commission has proposed an “Advanced Materials for Europe” agenda, setting out benchmark targets for 2035 intended to increase investment, company growth and the take-up of safer and more sustainable materials across the EU. The plan calls for the EU to become a global leader in inventing, producing and using advanced materials by 2035, with cooperation between member states designed to speed up the shift from laboratory research to products on the market, the Commission informed in a statement on Wednesday. Advanced materials are engineered at the level of atoms and can change how products perform, such as making them lighter, stronger or more energy efficient, the Commission said. t listed potential uses in sectors including energy, mobility, electronics, construction, health, aerospace and defence. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the initiative would help ensure “innovative materials created in Europe are also produced, scaled up and used in Europe.” The Commission set three benchmark targets for 2035: 20% more investment in advanced materials research and innovation, 20% more EU-based start-ups and scale-ups in the sector, and 20% of projects reaching higher deployment levels for safer and more sustainable advanced materials. New figures cited by the Commission put the current advanced materials sector at more than 15,000 companies, supporting around 1.5 million jobs across the EU. The proposal also sets out a framework for closer coordination between member states, including aligning investments and cutting the time between research and commercial application, the Commission said. It invited member states to work together on five priorities by 2030, including targeting research funding in strategic sectors, using digital tools and artificial intelligence to speed up discovery and testing, improving access to testing and pilot facilities, supporting scale-up through measures such as public procurement, and addressing skills through training and reskilling. The proposal requires adoption by the Council of the EU. Progress would be monitored using key performance indicators overseen by the Technology Council for Advanced Materials, with a first stocktake planned by the end of 2028 and a full implementation report by the end of 2030.
